Lessons.Title: Standard Algorithm: Multi-digit Numbers with Composing PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade5 U04:L06 is Standard Algorithm: Multi-digit Numbers with Composing PLC Activity. Use multi-digit factors and the standard algorithm with correct carrying in partial rows AND final addition. Prior source-aligned L05 lacked composing; this lesson changes the mathematical situation.

Warm-up Number Talk Three Factors: original (2×3)×10=60, (2×40)×10=800, (2×200)×10=4000 and (2×243)×10=4860. Pupil explains why tens factor 10 can be regrouped with the other factors without changing total.

Activity 1 Compose a New Unit: actual source 241×23=5543. Lin records 241×3=723 and 241×20=4820 then adds to 5543. The source asks what the 1 written above 241 represents in Lin's work: adding 7 hundreds and 8 hundreds creates 15 hundreds, hence one newly composed THOUSAND. It also asks learners to compute 182×41=7462 and 304×23=6992 by the standard algorithm. Original handwritten regrouping marks and reasoning require teacher review.

Activity 2 All the Products: original 647×9=5823, 647×50=32350, 647×59=38173 (sum of the first two), and 264×38=10032. Ask for correct columns, carry values and partial rows. Do not substitute the unrelated 273×24 source claim; retain that mathematically valid example only as an extension.

Independent Edulytiks Cool-down 372×46=17112 asks the pupil to show both partial rows and explain carried tens/hundreds. Exact selected numeric Practice cannot certify their original written standard algorithm. Original gated Cool-down and publisher figure artwork not independently verified.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Carry new units during multiplication
KeyConcepts.Definition: Ten of one place become one of the next larger place.
KeyConcepts.Rule: In 273×4, 4×3=12 creates 1 ten, and 4×7+1=29 creates 2 hundreds.

KeyConcepts.Title: The tens partial product
KeyConcepts.Definition: The second digit of a two-digit multiplier represents groups of ten.

KeyConcepts.Title: Add the two partial products
KeyConcepts.Definition: The standard algorithm sums ones-row and tens-row contributions after any carries.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Lin's 241×23
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain source Lin's 241×23=5543, the two rows and the carried 1.
WorkedExamples.Method: Source standard algorithm with partial rows and thousand carry.
Steps: Add 723+4820=5543; 7 hundreds+8 hundreds=15 hundreds, compose one thousand.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 5543; carried 1 denotes one thousand in the row addition.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source final products
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute 182×41,304×23,647×9,647×50,647×59 and 264×38.
WorkedExamples.Method: Place-value composing and correct tens shift.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original three-factor Number Talk
WorkedExamples.Question: Find (2×3)×10,(2×40)×10,(2×200)×10,(2×243)×10.
WorkedExamples.Method: Associativity and multiplication by ten.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — One composed two-row product
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 273×24, recording the new units.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Calculate 273×4=1092 and show the carried ten and hundreds.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Many compositions
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 368×57.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Find 368×50=18400 and explain the factor of ten.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Diagnose wrong tens alignment
WorkedExamples.Question: A pupil records 273×20 as 546. Explain what was omitted.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Interpret 20 as two tens, not two ones.
Multiply 273×2=546 only as an intermediate step.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The tens partial product should be 5460.
WorkedExamples.Check: The original full product must exceed the tens-row amount 5460.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat a carry as an extra digit with no unit
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A carried 2 in the hundreds column means two hundreds, not two ones.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Connect each carry to the result of multiplying units and regrouping.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Place the tens row in the ones column
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The second multiplier digit counts tens, not ones.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Shift the entire tens partial product one place to the left.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Present invented 273×24 as the textbook's Lin 241×23 algorithm or omit 647×59
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original source compares specific products and asks for what the written carried 1 represents.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore Lin's 241×23 and all source composing exercises with correct place-value explanations.

SummaryPoints: Source Lin 241×23=5543 from 723+4820; the carried 1 is a thousand.
Teacher reviews composing marks and source written algorithms; numeric choice is supplementary.

Lessons.Title: Build Multiplication Fluency
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade5 U04:L07 Build Multiplication Fluency: compare representations of an identical product, play a pupil-selected greater-product game using actual physical number cards, and optionally investigate carrying new units. Source number-card deck itself was not independently recovered from the teacher HTML and its numerical contents MUST NOT be fabricated as official original cards.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder Same Solution: two source standard-algorithm records show 417×28=11676 and 28×417=11676. One recording uses partial rows 3336 and 8340; another records 196,280,11200. Both are valid forms, demonstrating commutativity and place-value products; teacher reviews diagram details.

Activity 1 Greatest Product: the original game asks partners to choose number cards for a three-digit by two-digit multiplication, form valid numbers, compare products and award a point over five rounds. Teacher supplies the actual source cards, and learners explain their decisions. Existing Edulytiks 864×21,821×64,642×81 models remain explicitly FIRST-PARTY game examples only; their digits are not claimed as the source deck. Original strategy and card legality remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

Activity 2 optional Desperately Seeking 9 New Units: original source 256×5=1280,587×8=4696,809×9=7281. Determine how many tens and hundreds are carried in each and debate why a digit-by-digit 9×9=81 plus at most 8 previously carried yields at most 89, hence a single column can compose at most 8 new higher-place units, not 9. Student reasoning is teacher reviewed.

Independent Edulytiks teacher Cool-down 679×8=5432 asks for the full standard algorithm and newly composed units. Original publisher-gated Cool-down and any source number-card images remain unverified, so only exact known source arithmetic is selected Practice.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fluent multiplication with composing
KeyConcepts.Definition: Correctly retain new tens/hundreds across each partial product and its sum.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Carry composed units to the next place and check against an estimate.

KeyConcepts.Title: Digit-use product optimization
KeyConcepts.Definition: A legal product must use the available digits exactly once in the specified factor formats.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare full products rather than the apparent size of one factor.

KeyConcepts.Title: Largest ones-place carry
KeyConcepts.Definition: For multiplying two single digits at most 9, the result cannot exceed 81.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The largest new tens from a ones-place digit multiplication is 8.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original two equal 417×28 algorithms
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain why the source's two algorithms for 417×28 and 28×417 agree.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare two valid multiplication orders and their place-value partials.
Steps: Use commutativity and same total as check.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both exact source diagrams correspond to identical value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source compositions
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate 256×5,587×8 and 809×9 using the standard algorithm.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compose higher place units and explain carries.
WorkedExamples.Check: No digit multiplication plus carry needs to compose 9 of a new unit.

WorkedExamples.Title: Teacher-led source game versus independent model
WorkedExamples.Question: Describe the original five-round Greatest Product game and why an independent 821×64 vs 642×81 comparison is only an extension.
WorkedExamples.Method: Student partner chooses cards, records legal 3-digit×2-digit multiplications and justifies outcomes.
Steps: Partner A and B choose actual source cards in alternating turns.
Compare the two constructed whole-number products and award a point to larger value.
Teacher verifies card use and strategy; Edulytiks alternative 821×64=52544 vs642×81=52002.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Teacher-reviewed five-round game; the example favors 821×64 by 542.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original source card values not independently certified.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Compare a trial product
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute 864×21.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Revise the trial
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare 821×64 and 642×81 using the same five digits.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Compare the difference and discuss why factor positions matter.
WorkedExamples.Check: 52544−52002=542; these are compared trials, not a proven global maximum.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Check new tens from one digit product
WorkedExamples.Question: Can 9×9 compose nine tens?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Regroup 81 ones into 8 tens plus 1 one.
Recognize nine tens would require at least 90 ones.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume a largest-looking three-digit factor always creates the greatest legal product
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The two-digit multiplier can offset a decrease in the three-digit factor.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Evaluate complete products and explain candidate comparisons.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim a maximum after checking only two arrangements
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An optimization proof needs an exhaustive legal search or a valid mathematical exchange argument.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Classify trial products as examples unless a global proof has been supplied.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim independently chosen 1,2,4,6,8 game digits are the exact 2021 publisher number cards
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The teacher HTML describes choosing cards but does not expose the original deck, so specific invented digits are unsupported.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep source game directions and five-round rubric, label sample cards first-party and record source deck not verified.

SummaryPoints: Original source warmup 417×28=28×417=11676 with two partial-product decompositions.
Original partner Greatest Product uses actual source number cards and five rounds; deck values not independently certified.
Explain why standard algorithm cannot carry 9 of a newly composed unit in a single column.
Exact selected Practice supports known source numeric cases; teacher scores card games and carry arguments.

Lessons.Title: Multiplication Fluency
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade5 U04:L08 Multiplication Fluency: source learners choose one of two fluency games (Greatest Product OR Number Puzzles: Multiplication and Division), then use exactly the supplied digits 3,5,6,8,9 to make three-digit-by-two-digit whole-number products as close as possible to two source targets, 50000 and 20000. These are closeness optimizations, not always maxima.
Warm-up Number Talk The Distributive Property: original 6×15=90,6×17=102,6×2 1/3=14,6×2 2/3=16. Pupils explain 6×(2+1/3)=12+2 and 6×(2+2/3)=12+4, and connect mental multiplication strategies.

Activity 1 Fluency Practice Choice Time: teacher facilitates choice of source game, including strategy discussion and legal moves. Number Puzzle or Greatest Product outcomes vary by players; original complete card/deck material and physical implementation were not independently inspected, so do not invent a unique certified source winner.

Activity 2 Targeted Products: use original digits 3,5,6,8,9 once each in a three-digit factor and a two-digit factor. For TARGET 50000 an exact finite enumeration of 120 permutations gives 893×56=50008, ABSOLUTE difference 8. For TARGET 20000 the closest valid arrangement is 589×36=21204, difference 1204. These optimal candidate calculations are an Edulytiks mathematical verification of the printed constraint, not quotations from a source answer key; students still defend why their selected products are closer than other valid candidates.

Previously drafted 1,2,3,6,8 digit trials and a 40000 target are mathematically legitimate extra puzzles only, NOT the original 2021 Activity 2. Teacher reviews each legal digit use, choice of game, student strategy, estimation and closest-product proof. Edulytiks independent Cool-down is original reflection work, not a publisher Cool-down reproduction.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Target product versus largest product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Closest to a given target minimizes absolute difference, which may not maximize product.

KeyConcepts.Title: Use-once digits
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each of five given digits may be used once across a three-digit and a two-digit factor.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check one-to-one usage before validating the result.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distributive mental link
KeyConcepts.Definition: Known whole-number and mixed-number products can use the same decomposition structure.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source distributive Number Talk
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate 6×15,6×17,6×2 1/3 and 6×2 2/3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Break products into easy known facts, whole and fraction parts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source target 50000
WorkedExamples.Question: Arrange 3,5,6,8,9 once each for a three-digit×two-digit product near 50000.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare absolute distances to target; independently enumerate all 120 legal digit permutations to certify nearest.
Steps: Compute the absolute difference from target: 8.
A check of all 120 distinct permutations finds no closer product; teacher reviews the optimization argument.
WorkedExamples.Check: Digits 8,9,3,5,6 are all used exactly once.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source target 20000
WorkedExamples.Question: Use exactly 3,5,6,8,9 once to make a product closest to 20000.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare legal three- and two-digit arrangements, absolute distance from target.
Steps: Independent full permutation comparison finds this nearest under the printed slot constraints.
WorkedExamples.Check: All five source digits appear exactly once; no other legal arrangement is closer.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Compare closeness
WorkedExamples.Question: Which trial product is nearer 40000: 813×62 or 682×31?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Choose the smaller absolute difference, without claiming global optimality.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 813×62 is closer of these two trials.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Use a known fact
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute 6×2 2/3 mentally.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Check a new legal candidate
WorkedExamples.Question: Try 631×82 and compare to target 40000.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Verify digits 6,3,1,8,2 are all used once.
WorkedExamples.Check: It is farther than the 50406 trial (difference 10406).

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat the numerically greatest product as the closest to a target
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Distance from target depends on how far a candidate is above or below it.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Calculate absolute difference for every legal candidate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim optimality from checking a few trials
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source's exploration permits multiple strategies, but a mathematical minimum would require a complete proof.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label trial rankings honestly and continue revising or enumerate all candidates.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Replace source digits 3,5,6,8,9 and target 50000/20000 with invented 1,2,3,6,8 and 40000
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That creates a different optimization puzzle and does not cover both original 2021 source targets.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Present original source digits and target values first; preserve alternate puzzles only as clearly optional extensions.

SummaryPoints: Original source Activity1 choice: Greatest Product or Number Puzzles.
Original digits 3,5,6,8,9 used once per target to approach 50000 and 20000.
Edulytiks computed 893×56=50008 distance 8, and 589×36=21204 distance 1204, under source slots.
Teacher evaluates legal digit choices and qualitative nearest-product arguments, not only numeric values.

Lessons.Title: The Birds
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade 5 U04:L09 The Birds uses MULTIPLICATION in a realistic rectangular-prism VOLUME context. The source explicitly lists six bird species, floor side lengths and recommended height intervals; learners must estimate possible volumes then calculate minimum and maximum recommended volumes for EACH, reporting cubic inches rather than square inches.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder For the Birds: a source bird-house photograph is credited to US Fish and Wildlife Service Public Domain, but the exact image binary and display rights have not been independently verified. Teacher elicits visual observations, including possible sloped roofs; volume models the specified rectangular house interior rather than claiming exact roof shape.

Activity 1 Home is Where the Bird Lives: ORIGINAL table: chickadee 4×4 inch floor, height 6–10; wood duck 10×18, height 10–24; barn owl 10×18, height 15–18; red-headed woodpecker 6×6, height 12–15; bluebird 5×5, height 6–12; swallow 6×6, height 6–8. For each choose and explain an estimate consistent with width×length×a plausible height within the given source interval.

Activity 2 What is the Volume? Under the original rectangular-prism model, chickadee 96–160 cubic in; wood duck 1800–4320; barn owl 2700–3240; red-headed woodpecker 432–540; bluebird 150–300; swallow 216–288. Floor area is width×length in square inches, then multiplying by a height in inches produces CUBIC inches; teacher checks model limits, estimates and real world reasonableness.

Lesson source synthesis reviews the multiplication algorithm with 412×32=13184 (2×412=824 plus30×412=12360), but this does not replace the six birdhouse tasks. Earlier authored fictional 5×5 by height 7–11 and 8×9 by height 12–15 are OPTIONAL EXTENSIONS, not source table entries. Teacher checks open estimations and source picture interpretation. Independent Edulytiks Cool-down uses new birdhouse measurements.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Volume with a height interval
KeyConcepts.Definition: For positive fixed rectangular base area, volume increases with height.
KeyConcepts.Rule: base area×minimum height ≤ volume ≤ base area×maximum height.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choose a useful estimate
KeyConcepts.Definition: Estimate a viable height in the given range and multiply by a simple base area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For a height 7–11, 10 is a reasonable benchmark.

KeyConcepts.Title: Record correct cubic units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying square inches of floor by inches of height creates cubic inches.
KeyConcepts.Example: A linear answer alone cannot express the volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original chickadee recommended volumes
WorkedExamples.Question: A chickadee house floor is 4 by 4 inches and height 6–10 inches. Find the range.
WorkedExamples.Method: Volume of rectangular prism = floor area × height.
WorkedExamples.Check: All dimensions in inches; output must be cubic inches.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original wood duck and barn owl
WorkedExamples.Question: Two source species both use 10 by 18-inch floors but have different height ranges. Compute ranges.
WorkedExamples.Method: Both floor areas are 180 square inches; multiply by each height interval.
Steps: Compare volumes and interpret difference in recommended height.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Wood duck 1800–4320; barn owl 2700–3240 cubic inches.
WorkedExamples.Check: Shared floor does not imply shared volume range.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original remaining three species
WorkedExamples.Question: Find woodpecker, bluebird and swallow range of volumes from the printed source table.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute floor area and multiply by each printed min/max height.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Estimate a small birdhouse
WorkedExamples.Question: Floor 5 by 5 inches and height 7–11 inches. Find an approximate volume.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Choose a plausible height such as 10 inches.
WorkedExamples.Check: It lies between 175 and 275 cubic inches.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Find exact range
WorkedExamples.Question: Find minimum and maximum small birdhouse volumes.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Multiply by lower height 7 and upper height 11.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Compare larger birdhouse
WorkedExamples.Question: Floor 8 by 9 inches, height 12–15 inches. Find the range.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Compare dimensions and note these are for an ideal rectangular prism.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use one proposed height as the only possible valid answer
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source gives a range of possible heights.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Report estimated values and exact lower/upper bounds as distinct statements.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Include a pitched-roof shape in box volume without stating assumptions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A sloped roof is not a rectangular prism with the same uniform cross section.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Clarify what is modeled as a rectangular interior, and seek additional dimensions for other shapes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use a fictional 5×5 birdhouse with height 7–11 as the original 2021 source table
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source specifies six species and different fixed base sizes and height intervals; invented values lose all six contextual comparisons.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore all six original species and calculate minimum/maximum cubic volume for each; preserve fictional examples only as extensions.

SummaryPoints: Source original six birdhouse species and printed floor/height intervals are included, not fictional substitutions.
Exact source ranges (in³): chickadee96–160,wood duck1800–4320,barn owl2700–3240,woodpecker432–540,bluebird150–300,swallow216–288.
Open plausible estimates and original source photograph remain teacher reviewed.
Source lesson synthesis 412×32=13184 retains place-value multiplication connection.
Independent Cool-down new floor7×8 in and height9–12 gives504–672 cubic inches.

Lessons.Title: World’s Record Folk Dance
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use the meaning of division to find how many equal-sized groups make up a multi-thousand-person event, applying multiplication as an inverse check and comparing group sizes. The 2021 source intentionally permits many student strategies before formal partial-quotients algorithms are established in later lessons.

Warm-up: discuss an original picture-free event model consisting of 60 groups of eight participants plus four additional groups. Ask students how many participants that represents and what repeating group sizes reveal about the array; the source dance photo and event-specific images are not copied.

Activity 1 — original example with changed numbers: an imagined folk-dance celebration has 3,456 dancers arranged in groups of eight. Begin with 400 groups×8=3200, leaving 256. Add 30 groups×8=240 and 2 groups×8=16; so 400+30+2=432 groups. Explain every partial number in context and verify 432×8=3456.

Activity 2 — keep the same number of dancers but use groups of four and two. There are 3456÷4=864 four-dancer groups and 3456÷2=1728 two-dancer groups. Explain by regrouping why each group-of-eight creates two groups of four and four groups of two, so the number of groups doubles and quadruples.

Teacher review: the source's world record event asks for a learner-selected division strategy, comparing it against other people's methods, and relating changed divisors to changed groups. Exact quotients are machine-checkable but cannot replace the explanation and interpretation. No source-specific protected photograph or gated response copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Division counts equal groups
KeyConcepts.Definition: Given a total and equal group size, divide to determine the number of groups.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial quotient approach
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtract known multiples of the divisor and add the number of groups accounted for.

KeyConcepts.Title: Change group size
KeyConcepts.Definition: With a fixed positive total, halving positive group size doubles the number of groups.
KeyConcepts.Example: 864 groups of four versus 432 groups of eight.

WorkedExamples.Title: How many groups of eight?
WorkedExamples.Question: 3456 dancers join groups of eight. How many groups?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: The remaining 256 dancers include 30 groups (240) and 2 groups (16).

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare groups of four
WorkedExamples.Question: The same 3456 dancers form groups of four. How many?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Every group of eight can be divided into two groups of four.
Verify by multiplying the quotient by four.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare groups of two
WorkedExamples.Question: How many pairs can 3456 dancers make?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the mathematical structure with first-party place-value or contextual representations.
Steps: Each group of four makes two pairs.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Divide groups by the number of participants instead of participants by group size
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The dividend is the known total number of people, not the unknown group count.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the total and desired size of each group before writing the expression.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim fewer people per group means fewer groups
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: With a fixed positive total, smaller groups mean more groups.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Relate groups of eight to two groups of four or four groups of two.

SummaryPoints: Division and multiplication describe the same grouping relationship.
Partial quotient groups can be combined into an exact quotient.
Method choice, contextual labels and comparisons require teacher review.
